scenes.vo: A forty-dollar mug set arrives with a chip on the rim. Today, that means a return: a label, a trip to the post office, and a week of waiting for your money.
For the store, it's worse. They refund all forty dollars, pay eight more to ship back a mug they'll throw away, and still lose a little of the customer's trust.
ClipPay settles damage claims with one photo and a partial PayPal refund. The buyer keeps the item. Nothing gets shipped back.
The buyer opens their claim and gets a four-character code. They write it on paper and photograph it next to the damage. That proves the photo is fresh, and that it's theirs.
The AI looks at the photo: what's damaged, where, how badly, whether it's a real photo, and whether the code matches.

But the AI never sets the price. A rules engine turns the grade into an offer using the merchant's own policy: a percentage for each severity, a ceiling, and an auto-approve limit. Thirty-five tests make sure the model can never talk its way into a bigger refund.
The buyer sees one clear offer. They can accept it, or counter once. A small counter is approved on the spot. Anything bigger goes to a person.
Then PayPal sends a partial refund on the original payment, with an idempotency key, so a retry can never pay twice. Photo to money in under a minute.
Merchants see every claim in one dashboard: what they refunded, what they saved compared with full returns, and a short queue of claims that need a human, like a missing code or a reused photo.

Now the real thing, live in the PayPal sandbox. We buy the mug set and pay with PayPal. The claim gives us a code, and we photograph it next to the damage. This crack is too severe to settle automatically, so the rules engine caps the refund and sends it to the merchant. One click, and the partial refund shows up in PayPal. That's the real app, end to end.
It's live today on Cloudflare, with PayPal payments and AI grading. ClipPay. Keep the item. Keep the customer.
